Hook: In 1930, in the first year of the Great Depression, John Maynard Keynes wrote an essay for his grandchildren. We are suffering just now, he wrote, from a bad attack of economic pessimism. He looked a hundred years ahead instead. In a hundred years, he wrote, the standard of life in the progressive countries will be between four and eight times as high as it is today. And people will work perhaps fifteen hours a week, in three-hour shifts, because the economic problem will be close to solved. The real problem will be how to use the freedom. On the way, he warned of a new disease, technological unemployment: unemployment due to our discovery of ways to economise on labour, outrunning the pace at which we find new uses for labour. The hundred years are up in 2030.

How did he do? On the first forecast, very well. In six of the countries he would have called progressive, GDP per head in 2022 was between 4.4 and 7.4 times its level of 1930. Inside his range, and with eight years to spare. On the second, not at all. Fifteen hours a week is about seven hundred and eighty hours a year. Hours did fall: in Germany from about 2,427 a year in 1950 to 1,335. But nowhere is close to Keynes's line, and in the United States hours have hardly moved since the nineteen-eighties. We took most of our riches as more things, not more time.

Now the machines are learning to do more than the economising Keynes imagined. The question of this part: what happens to work, growth and incomes if machines can do most tasks? Which tasks do machines take, and which new ones appear? Why do general-purpose technologies take decades to show up in productivity? What do the experiments with AI assistants find, and for whom? How do task-level gains add up, and what happens to wages? And could automating research itself make growth explode?
Economics, Built. Part sixty-five: the economics of AI.

Part sixty-four was about machines that help economists. This part is about machines that change the economy. By the end you will know the task model, in which automation displaces workers, raises productivity, and is offset by new tasks, and what that does to wages and labour's share; why general-purpose technologies take decades to pay, and why measured productivity first falls; what the experiments with AI assistants find, and the arithmetic that turns task-level gains into an economy-wide number; what happens to growth when research itself is automated, why the tasks left to people set the pace, and how to test for an explosion in the data; and who captures the gains, what happens when software trades with software, and what policy can do.
PlayIt: Chapter one. Play it: automate the lab.

Your turn. Here is an economy whose growth comes from ideas, and ideas come from research. Research is a long list of tasks: designing, testing, checking, writing up. Each task can be done by researchers, whose number grows one percent a year with the population, or, once it is automated, by machines, of which there are as many as the economy's capital allows. The tasks are complements: every one of them has to be done. With no automation the economy grows about 3 percent a year per person, for ever. Now automate a share of the research tasks: none, half, three quarters, ninety percent, or all. For each, what is the growth rate a century from now?

Here is what the model does. With no automation, growth stays near 3 percent. Automate half the tasks, and growth jumps, to about 7 percent within 13 years, because machines multiply as capital grows. Then it falls back. At three quarters, and at ninety percent, the boom is bigger and longer: ninety percent reaches about 24 percent a year around year 43. But a century on it is back to 7 percent and still falling. Automate every task, and growth does not fall back. It explodes, passing fifty percent a year by year 49, where we stopped the model. The reason is the most important idea in this part. With complementary tasks, the ones machines cannot do become the bottleneck. As machines get cheap, the work left to people takes over the cost of research, and its slow growth sets the pace. Only when no task is left does the bottleneck disappear.
History: Chapter two. Technology and work, historically.

Machines have taken work before. Between 1811 and 1816, framework knitters in the English Midlands broke the stocking frames that were cutting their piece rates. Parliament made frame-breaking a capital crime, and sent soldiers. The word Luddite has meant a fool ever since. But in 1821 David Ricardo, the most rigorous economist of his day, added a chapter to his Principles called On Machinery. He had been wrong, he wrote: the labourers' fear that machinery would hurt them was not founded on prejudice, but on the correct principles of political economy. A machine can raise the owner's income and lower the workers', at least for a while.

He was right about the while. Here is England, indexed to 1770: in gold, GDP per head; in pink, a labourer's real wage. Through the decades of the new machines, output per head rose, and wages did not follow. By 1840 GDP per head was about 35 percent above its 1770 level, the real wage about 17 percent, after falling below it around 1800. Robert Allen called it Engels's pause, after the man who watched it from Manchester, and Part nineteen met it. Then wages caught up, and for a century and a half rose with output. Both halves of the story matter: the long run was good for workers, and the short run lasted a working life.

There is a darker precedent. In the first half of the twentieth century, tractors replaced the horses and mules that had pulled American ploughs. There were tens of millions of them. Nobody retrained them. In 1983 Wassily Leontief, a Nobel laureate, warned that the role of humans as a factor of production might diminish in the same way. So far, people are not horses. A horse could only pull. When machines took over pulling, and then spinning and adding, people moved to tasks machines could not do, and new tasks kept being invented. Whether that remains true is the question of this part.

A modern example shows how. Cash machines spread through American banks from the nineteen-seventies. Timothy Hannan and Gerald Hanweck, at the Federal Reserve, counted the staff of a commercial bank's urban branch: about twenty in 1988, a little over thirteen by 2004. But a branch with fewer staff is cheaper to run, so banks opened more of them: between 1988 and 2006 the number of commercial bank branches rose by thirty-nine percent. James Bessen showed that the tellers' work changed with it: less counting of cash, more selling and advice. And across the economy, David Autor and coauthors find that about sixty percent of American jobs in 2018 had titles that did not exist in 1940. Machines take tasks; economies invent new ones. The economics of AI is a race between the two.
Tasks: Economists think about this race with a model of tasks, from Joseph Zeira and, in its modern form, Daron Acemoglu and Pascual Restrepo. Output needs a range of tasks, from N minus one to N, combined with an elasticity sigma below one: the tasks are complements. Machines can do the tasks below a threshold I; people do the rest. Automation moves I to the right. People lose those tasks: that is displacement. But the automated tasks get cheaper, output rises, and so does the demand for people in the tasks they still do: the productivity effect. And the economy invents new tasks, in which people have the advantage: N moves right, the oldest tasks drop away, and people gain work: reinstatement.

The model gives the wage in one line. The log wage is one over sigma times log output, the productivity effect, plus one over sigma times the log of the range of tasks people do, the displacement effect. Run it with capital fixed, in the short run, and automate from a fifth of the tasks to 67 percent, the point where machines stop being cheaper than people. Output rises: productivity adds 67 log points to the wage. People's range of tasks shrinks: displacement subtracts 109. Net, the wage falls by 42 log points. Automation is not a free lunch for workers. Whether it helps them depends on whether the productivity effect is bigger than the displacement.

Now let the automation frontier sweep from a fifth of the tasks to four fifths. With capital fixed, the wage first rises, as cheap machines raise output, then falls, as people are pushed into fewer tasks, until machines are no longer cheaper and automation stops. In the long run capital is built to meet demand, at a fixed rental, and the productivity effect wins: the wage rises the whole way. But labour's share of output falls in both. In the long run, from 81 percent to 23. Higher wages, a smaller slice. Then let new tasks arrive, in which people are more productive than in the old ones. Labour's share climbs back to 62 percent, and the wage rises by another 24 percent. Acemoglu and Restrepo's reading of American history is that, until the late nineteen-eighties, new tasks kept pace with automation; since then, they have not.

Which automation is good for workers? Automate ten percent more of the tasks, in the long run, and vary what the machine costs. If machines are far cheaper than people, the productivity effect is large: the wage rises by about 53 percent. If machines are barely cheaper, the displacement is the same, and labour's share falls by the same 9 or so points, but the gain is tiny: 3 percent. Acemoglu and Restrepo call this so-so automation: self-checkout machines that save the shop a little and take a whole task from people. The worry about AI is not that it is brilliant. It is that much of it could be so-so.

The evidence from earlier waves fits the model. Across American commuting zones, Acemoglu and Restrepo find that one more industrial robot per thousand workers lowered the employment-to-population ratio by about 0.2 percentage points and wages by 0.42 percent. And they attribute between half and seventy percent of the change in the American wage structure from 1980 to 2016 to groups whose routine tasks were automated. That is the polarization of Part thirty-nine: computers took routine tasks and helped with abstract ones. What is new about generative AI is where it reaches: writing, coding, advising, the non-routine cognitive tasks the last wave left to people, often to the best paid.
GPT: Economists call technologies like electricity, the computer and now AI general-purpose technologies: they can be used almost everywhere, they keep improving for decades, and they pay only once new inventions, processes and skills grow up around them. Paul David asked in 1990 why the electric dynamo took so long to pay. In 1899, almost two decades after the first power stations, electric motors supplied under five percent of the mechanical drive in American factories. The old factory was built around a steam engine and a line shaft: every machine had to sit along the shaft, often on several floors. Swapping the engine for one big electric motor saved little. The gain came when each machine got its own small motor, and the factory could be laid out around the flow of the work, on one floor. That meant new buildings, new processes and new skills. By 1929, motors supplied about seventy-eight percent of the drive, and manufacturing productivity surged in the nineteen-twenties.

Erik Brynjolfsson, Daniel Rock and Chad Syverson turned this into a measurement problem. A general-purpose technology needs complementary investment: reorganization, training, software firms write for themselves. Most of it is intangible, and the national accounts miss much of it. While firms build it, the work they put in shows up as cost, not output, so measured productivity falls: here by about 6 percent, at the bottom of the J. Later the intangible capital pays, but because it was never counted as an input, its returns look like productivity growth: measured productivity ends 13 percent above the old path, the truth 7. They call it the productivity J-curve: early on, the statistics understate a new technology; later, they overstate it.

In 1987 Robert Solow wrote that you can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics. He was right at the time. American output per hour grew 2.8 percent a year from 1948 to 1973, then only 1.4 percent until 1995, while computers spread. Then, a decade after his remark, it showed up: 3.0 percent a year from 1995 to 2004, much of it from producing and using computers. And then it faded again, to 1.5 percent until 2019. Since 2019, 2.3 percent. Whether AI is behind any of that recent pickup is too early to say, and the J-curve warns that the first years of a general-purpose technology are exactly when the statistics are least reliable.
Experiments: Chapter five. What the experiments find.

Since 2023 economists have run randomized experiments with AI assistants. Shakked Noy and Whitney Zhang gave ChatGPT to half of about four hundred and fifty professionals writing press releases, reports and emails: time per task fell forty percent, and graders rated the work eighteen percent better. Programmers given GitHub's Copilot built a small web server fifty-six percent faster. Consultants at Boston Consulting Group, on tasks the model could do well, finished a quarter faster and did twelve percent more of them. At a software firm's customer support desk, five thousand agents given an assistant resolved fourteen percent more problems per hour. And in 2025 METR randomized real issues for sixteen experienced open-source developers, in code they knew well. With AI allowed, they took nineteen percent longer, while believing it had made them faster. Short, well-defined tasks show large gains; long work in a familiar, complicated setting, so far, may not. METR has since said its estimate is probably out of date, as the tools have improved.

The most striking pattern is who gains. On the Island we built a support desk like Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond's: 2,000 agents of differing skill, half given an assistant at random, with an effect we planted. The experiment recovers the average: about 15 percent more resolutions per hour. And it recovers the pattern: the least skilled fifth gains about 33 percent, the most skilled almost nothing. In the real study, the newest and least skilled agents gained about a third, and the best saw small gains in speed and small falls in quality. The assistant had learned from the best agents' conversations, and passed their know-how to the rest. So the gap between the top and bottom fifths shrinks, from 1.85 to 1.38. Noy and Zhang found the same compression in writing. Within a job, at least at first, these tools are levellers.

The consulting study adds a warning. On tasks inside what its authors called the frontier of the model's abilities, consultants with GPT-4 were faster and more productive, and graders rated their work much better. But they also set a task chosen to look easy while lying just outside the frontier. There, consultants using the model were nineteen percentage points less likely to get the right answer than those without it. They trusted it where they should not have. Fabrizio Dell'Acqua and coauthors call it a jagged frontier: which side a task falls on is hard to see in advance, and it moves with every new model. And all these studies measure time on a set task. They do not measure the value of the work, what people learn or stop learning, or what happens to the jobs. For that we need the aggregates.
Aggregates: Chapter six. From tasks to aggregates.

To go from a task to the economy, first ask how many tasks AI could touch. Tyna Eloundou, Sam Manning, Pamela Mishkin and Daniel Rock rated every task in the American occupational database, with human raters and with a model, asking whether a language model could cut the time it takes by half. About eighty percent of American workers, they found, could have at least a tenth of their tasks affected; about nineteen percent, at least half. And exposure rises with pay, the opposite of the robots, which reached the factory floor first. But exposure is a judgement that a task could be sped up. It is not adoption, and it is not a forecast of jobs lost.

Then use the theorem of Part sixty-three. Hulten's theorem says that, to a first approximation, a saving in some part of the economy raises total factor productivity by the share of GDP it touches times the saving. Daron Acemoglu did this arithmetic in 2024. About a fifth of tasks are exposed. Of those, he took about twenty-three percent as worth doing with AI within ten years, from a study of when computer vision pays. That is about four and a half percent of GDP. From the experiments, a saving of about twenty-seven percent of labour costs, and labour is a little over half of those tasks' costs: a cost saving of about fourteen percent. Multiply: about two thirds of one percent higher productivity, after ten years. Less than a tenth of a percentage point a year. Allowing for harder tasks, his estimate falls to about half a percent.

Other forecasts are many times larger. Joseph Briggs and Devesh Kodnani at Goldman Sachs projected one and a half percentage points a year of extra American labour productivity growth, for a decade, with wide adoption. Philippe Aghion and Simon Bunel, reasoning from electricity and the computer, got between 0.8 and 1.3 points a year. The same arithmetic shows what separates them. Keep a fifth of tasks exposed, but let sixty percent of them adopt, at a saving of forty percent: 2.6 percent over ten years. Let half of all tasks be exposed, and all of them adopt: 11 percent, about one point a year. To get the large numbers, AI has to reach far more of the economy than today's experiments, or do something the formula leaves out: speed up the invention of new products and ideas. That is the subject of chapter eight.

Here is the whole map, at the experiments' twenty-seven percent saving. Across, the share of tasks exposed; up, the share of those adopted; the colour, the gain in productivity after ten years. Acemoglu's inputs sit in the dark corner. The bright corner needs most of the economy to be exposed and nearly all of it to adopt. Where the economy lands is an empirical question, and the next decade's data will answer it. Watch the adoption share: it is the number the experiments cannot give.
Wages: Chapter seven. Wages and labour's share.

The task model's warning is about labour's share of income. In the United States it was about 63 percent of GDP in 1950, by the Penn World Table's measure. By 2023 it was about 57 percent, most of the fall since 2000. Part thirty-nine weighed the suspects: automation, superstar firms that make a lot with few workers, and trade. Six points of GDP is a great deal of money. But it is not the end of work. The question is what happens if machines can do every task.

Take the task model and let capital accumulate, year by year, as people save. Anton Korinek and Donghyun Suh asked what happens to wages under different paths for the automation frontier. In grey, business as usual: the frontier creeps forward, but the hardest tasks keep receding ahead of it. Capital piles up, and the wage rises, from 1.25 to 2.60 in sixty years. In orange, every task becomes automatable within twenty years. For a couple of years the wage edges up; then it falls, and from year 11 it sits at one. In red, every task in five years: the wage falls almost at once, to the same level. Labour's share collapses in both, from 73 percent to 6. And output? In sixty years it grows 11-fold when every task is automated, 2.5-fold under business as usual. A far richer economy, in which work earns almost none of the income.

Why does the wage stop at one, in this model? Because a firm will automate a task whenever a machine is cheaper per unit of work, the wage per unit of a person's work can never stay above the cost of a machine's for long, once machines can do everything. A person is worth what the machine that could replace them costs. That is not zero: people still produce what they did. But the wage stops growing with the economy, however rich the economy gets. If some essential tasks stay human, the opposite happens: their scarcity raises their pay, the same bottleneck as in the Play-it. Korinek and Suh show that whether wages collapse or keep rising depends on whether the list of tasks only people can do runs out. Either way, more of the income goes to whoever owns the machines. The distribution of capital becomes the distribution of income, and Part forty's questions become the central ones.
Research: Chapter eight. Growth with automated research.

Chapter six's arithmetic treats AI as a cheaper way to do today's tasks. The bigger question is whether it changes how fast we invent. Recall the model of ideas from Part twenty-one. New ideas come from researchers, S, standing on the shoulders of the ideas already found, A. But ideas get harder to find: phi is below one. Nicholas Bloom, Charles Jones, John Van Reenen and Michael Webb found that keeping Moore's law going now takes more than eighteen times as many researchers as in the early nineteen-seventies. So in the long run, growth is tied to the growth of the number of researchers, which is tied to the growth of the population. Now suppose machines can be researchers.

Philippe Aghion, Benjamin Jones and Charles Jones wrote this down. Research is a set of tasks, a share beta done by machines and the rest by people, combined with an elasticity below one. Automate ninety percent, and growth booms, as in the Play-it: to about 24 percent a year. Now watch where the money goes. At first, the machines' tasks are most of the cost of research, and the people's ten percent is almost nothing. But machines multiply, their tasks get cheap, and the people's tasks, which cannot be skipped, take over the cost: by year 41 they are half of it, and soon nearly all. From then on, research grows only as fast as the people doing the last tasks, and growth falls back. This is William Baumol's cost disease, from 1967, in the laboratory: the tasks that are hard to improve end up determining the pace.

The same logic applies to the whole economy. Two goods that people want together, like food and haircuts. Automate the making of one, so its productivity grows 6 percent a year, while the other's grows 0.5. The automated good gets cheaper and cheaper, and because people do not want ever more of it, its share of spending falls, from half to 7 percent in a century. Aggregate growth is the average of the two sectors' growth, weighted by spending, so it slides from 3.2 percent towards the slow sector's 0.5. Agriculture and manufacturing went this way: brilliant productivity, shrinking shares of GDP. William Nordhaus found the pattern across American industries. Automation that leaves an essential task to people can make that task the economy's pace-setter.

So which is it? The case for explosive growth is the Play-it's last line: if AI can do every task in research, including improving AI, ideas produce the machines that produce ideas, and growth accelerates. The case against is the bottleneck: experiments in the physical world take time, compute needs chips and power, regulation moves slowly, and any task still left to people sets the pace. The models agree on what to watch: whether the share of tasks automated, in research above all, approaches one, or stalls short of it. The stakes are the difference between Part twenty-one's two percent a year and a world economy that doubles in a few years. The models allow both. The data have to decide.
Nordhaus: William Nordhaus asked how we would know. For growth to explode, he showed, information capital, computers and software and now AI, must substitute for people well enough: the elasticity of substitution between them must be above one, either in production or in what people buy. If it is, then as computing gets cheaper, it leaves signatures in the data: productivity growth should accelerate, capital's share of income should rise, and information capital should become a growing share of all capital. So look for the signatures, and ask how long they would take to get there.

Here are three of his signatures, on today's data. First, American productivity growth by decade: 2.2 percent a year in the nineteen-nineties, 2.7 in the two-thousands, 1.5 in the twenty-tens, 1.7 since 2020. No acceleration. Second, capital's share of income: 37 percent in 1950, 43 in 2023. Rising, which points the right way. Third, the price of computing: the number of transistors on a chip has doubled about every 2 years for half a century. Computing has never been cheaper, and that is the fuel. The question is whether it substitutes for people fast enough to show up in the first two.

Nordhaus's own verdict, on data to the late twenty-tens, was that the singularity is not near. Most of his tests pointed away from it. A couple pointed towards it, but at their pace it was many decades off. Since then, productivity growth has picked up a little, capital's share is high, and generative AI arrived after his data ended. Called it? His tests are the right ones to run again every year. For now: too early to say.
Market: Who will capture the gains? Start with costs. Training a frontier model is an enormous fixed cost: months of computation on tens of thousands of chips. Epoch AI's records show the compute used to train frontier models growing four to five times a year since 2010. Serving one more answer costs little, and the price of a given level of capability has fallen fast. A cost that is mostly fixed favours a few large producers: the natural monopoly of Part ten, and the platforms of Part forty-four. But there are forces the other way. Followers can learn from the leaders' outputs, open-weight models can be run by anyone, and users switch between models with a click. Anton Korinek and Jai Vipra map these forces in detail.

A toy makes the arithmetic plain. With Cournot competition on a linear demand, each of N firms earns the market size M over N plus one squared. Entry stops when that no longer covers the fixed cost F of a frontier model: at about the square root of M over F, minus one. Suppose the market doubles each year, but the cost of staying at the frontier triples. The market supports 9 frontier firms in the first year, 4 after three years, and 1 by the end. If the cost of the frontier grows faster than the market for it, the frontier narrows to a very few firms. Below it, a competitive layer of older and open models, priced near cost. These are invented numbers. The point is the race between two growth rates, which the industry's next few years will measure.

AI is made along a chain. Chips, data centres, the model makers, the applications built on the models, and finally users and workers. The surplus goes to whoever is scarcest along the chain. Today, chips and electricity are scarce, and models compete hard, so the price of a given capability keeps falling. If models stay close to one another, most of the gains pass to the people who use them, as consumer surplus, much of which GDP does not count: Part three's free goods. If one model pulls far ahead, or owns the data and the customers, the questions of Part forty-four, lock-in, tying and self-preferencing, return at a larger scale.
Policy: Policy begins with fear, and fear begins with forecasts. Called it? In 2013 Carl Benedikt Frey and Michael Osborne classified seven hundred and two occupations by how easily their tasks could be computerised, and concluded that about forty-seven percent of American employment was at high risk, perhaps over a decade or two. It became one of the most cited numbers of the decade. Since September 2013, American payroll employment has risen by about 16 percent. But the paper rated what was technically possible, not what would be adopted or when, and its second decade is not over. Too early to say. The lesson of the task model holds: technically automatable is not automated. Cost, adoption and new tasks decide.

Should robots be taxed? Bill Gates suggested it in 2017, to replace the income tax lost when robots replace workers. Joao Guerreiro, Sergio Rebelo and Pedro Teles worked it out in a model with routine and non-routine workers. Automation does not shrink the tax base, they found; it raises output and revenue. The reason to tax robots is different: workers already in routine occupations, too far into their careers to retrain, lose; and a tax on robots raises their wages, which an income tax cannot target. So the optimal tax is modest, and falls to zero once the current generation of routine workers has retired. The curve here shows only its shape. The case is about distribution, and it is temporary.

Beyond robot taxes, six levers. Insure the people who lose, with the tools of Part forty-two, sized for a displacement that may come faster than past ones. If income moves from work to capital, who owns the capital matters: pensions, broad ownership, the taxes of Parts forty and forty-one. Keep the markets of chapter ten open. Steer the technology: Daron Acemoglu, Andrea Manera and Pascual Restrepo argue that the American tax code taxes labour much more heavily than equipment and software, which tilts firms towards automating; and Acemoglu and Simon Johnson argue that research could aim at helping workers rather than replacing them. Educate for the tasks that complement machines, the race of Part thirty-nine. And measure: the statistics will lag the change.

And here, as always, the line between what economics can show and what it cannot. Economics can show that automation can raise output while lowering some workers' wages and labour's share, and that policy can move income from winners to losers, at some cost. Whether to slow automation, tax it, or let it run and compensate, needs value judgments: how much a displaced worker's loss weighs against everyone else's gain; whether work matters beyond its pay; how much faster growth is worth against a fairer share of it. Those are yours to make. The models tell you what each choice costs.
Agents: Now let the software trade. Start with buyers. Hal Varian's model of sales, from 1980, has two kinds of buyer: shoppers, who compare every price, and the rest, who buy from the first shop they meet. Here, 4 sellers, a full price of one and a cost of 0.4. Sellers cannot settle on one price: they mix, running random sales to catch the shoppers while charging the others a lot. Now give a growing share of buyers an agent that checks every price. The prices sellers charge fall, the agents find the lowest, and the average price paid falls in a straight line, from the full price towards cost. The formula is exact: sellers earn just what they would by selling only to the buyers without agents, at the full price. A world in which every buyer has an agent is close to perfect competition.

Sellers can have agents too. In Part forty-four, simple learning algorithms set prices against each other and, with no instruction to collude and no messages, settled well above the competitive price, punishing undercutting with price wars. Sara Fish, Yannai Gonczarowski and Ran Shorrer gave the same job to agents built on language models. They reached prices above competition quickly, and seemingly harmless changes to the wording of their instructions changed how far. Cartel law punishes agreements. Software that learns to avoid price wars agrees on nothing. A market where both sides are software could be more competitive than any before, or less, depending on whose agents are smarter.

This brings back the questions of market design. When a polished cover letter costs nothing to write, it stops signalling effort or interest: the signals of Part thirteen work only while they are costly. When agents can apply, bid and message at no cost, the markets of Part seventeen will need limits on how many, like the caps on applications in school choice. Who is bound by a contract an agent signs, and who pays when it makes a mistake? And markets everywhere may come to clear at machine speed, with the arms race that high-frequency trading brought to finance.
Dials: Chapter thirteen. The Dials: AI on tasks, AI in aggregate.

This part opens two Dials. The first: the effect of generative AI on a task, measured as the studies report it, in time saved or output per hour. Writing: forty percent less time. A small coding job: 56 percent less, with a wide interval. Consulting tasks inside the frontier: a quarter faster. Customer support: fourteen percent more resolutions per hour. Experienced developers in their own code, in early 2025: nineteen percent slower. And the Island's desk, where the truth is planted: 15 percent. The status: depends on the setting. The gains are large on short, well-defined tasks and for the least experienced, and can turn negative where the work is long, familiar and complicated.

The second Dial: AI's addition to productivity growth over the next decade, in percentage points a year. Acemoglu's arithmetic: 0.07, less with hard tasks. Aghion and Bunel, with the same formula and a broader reading of the experiments: a median of 0.68, with a range from almost nothing to over a point. By analogy with electricity and computers: 0.8 to 1.3. Goldman Sachs, with widespread adoption: one and a half. The status: contested. The estimates differ by a factor of twenty, mostly because they assume different adoption, and none includes AI's effect on the rate of invention, which could dwarf them all, or come to nothing.
